senses: A restaurant that specializes in crêpes.
Synonym of reverberant (“that tends to reverberate (“(repeatedly) bounce against one or more surfaces”) or has reverberated”); re-echoed.
ety: Borrowed from Latin reverberātus, see Etymology 1 and -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more. etymology 2, adjective sense 2 (“ringing or vibrating with many echoing sounds”) was popularized by its use in Twelfth Night (written c. 1601–1602; published 1623) by the English playwright William Shakespeare (1564–1616): see the quotation.

senses: Tending to cut or tear.
ety: From Middle English scherynge; equivalent to shear + -ing.

senses: To hit something better or further than (another), especially to score better in a game involving hitting a ball with a bat.
examples: Nitschke could see that the Chiefs were another team like the Cowboys, a team that tried to outcute the defense rather than outhit them.

senses: A neurological disorder in which the person affected has an abnormally small head due to a failure of brain growth.
A collapsible top hat.
ety: From the surname of its French inventor.

senses: A contrasting border around a shield.
ety: A collateral form of, and thus a doublet of border (from Middle English bordure).

senses: One who, or that which, discerns, distinguishes, or judges.
examples: A great observer and discerner of men's natures.

senses: naval military power
The seeds of wild rue.
examples: Not only is esfand directly endorsed by God and used by the Prophet Muhammad, but it also instills courage, expels demons and diseases, and repels the evil eye.
The inhibitive role of Esfand seed extract (ESE) was studied in 3.5% NaCl medium.
Alkaloids of Esfand can form dangerous reaction with antihistamines, antidepressants, decongestants, expectorant and some stimulants

senses: An Aboriginal person living according to tradition.
The support of advocacy of a union, especially of a trade union.
Support for the North (the Union) during the American Civil War.
Support for the continuance of the United Kingdom (especially with respect to Northern Ireland).
A reverberatory furnace.
ety: Borrowed from New Latin reverberatorius; by surface analysis, reverberate + -ory.

senses: Someone who irons, someone who does ironing.
A mangle, a device used to iron clothes.
Obtained simultaneously over a wide area, for presenting a comprehensive and nearly instantaneous picture of the state of the atmosphere.
ety: From New Latin synopticus, from Ancient Greek συνοπτικός (sunoptikós, “seeing the whole together or at a glance”), from σύνοψις (súnopsis, “a general view, synopsis”), from συν- (sun-, “with”) + ὄψις (ópsis, “view”).

senses: plain or simple twilled fabric
a draft garment made of inexpensive cloth for the purposes of fitting and design evaluation
ety: Borrowed from French toile. Doublet of tela.

senses: Having a tendency to steal.
Having the manner of a thief; furtive; stealthy.
ety: From Middle English thevysch, equivalent to thief + -ish. Cognate with Saterland Frisian däifsk (“thievish”), Dutch diefs (“thievish”), German Low German deevsk (“thievish”), German diebisch (“thievish”).

senses: To hug and snuggle simultaneously: gesture of tender non-sexual affection.
To hug and cuddle.
A sweet wine, especially from Germany, made from late harvest grapes; specifically, a wine from the German official Auslese category.
Brazilian jiu-jitsu, a related art, derived from judo.
Strategic maneuvering, especially with the aim of using the strength of one's opponent against them in an unexpected or counterintuitive way.
ety: Borrowed from Japanese 柔術 (jūjutsu). Popular spelling jitsu (instead of less popular jiutsu or jutsu) could reference to allophonic [d͡ʑɨ] or [d͡ʑi] (in Shitamachi dialect). First mentioned in The Japan Mail (1875, page 133), before the widespread use of the Hepburn system.

senses: Synonym of geisha.
ety: Borrowed from Japanese 芸子 (geiko) (from the Kyoto dialect).

senses: A type of luxury fabric with a background weft.
The condition or state of being reflexive.
A wine imitating those of Sauternes.
ety: A deliberate misspelling by American vintners of the name of the famed French wine region Sauternes and the wines they produce.

senses: A high, desert landscape from which most of the sand has been removed by wind erosion
The rootstock of the bloodroot, once used medicinally as an emetic, etc.
Having a bad smell.
examples: The whiffy smell of the compost pile made me turn away.
The clothes smelled whiffy after being left in the damp laundry room.

senses: Characteristic of, or suitable to, a cousin
To grow or sprout.
To spread abnormally.
To live or spend a period of time in a dull, inactive, unchallenging way.
ety: Borrowed from Latin vegetātus, perfect passive participle of vegetō (“to enliven, to arouse”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).

senses: A large bronze or (rarely) small silver coin minted during the Roman Republic and Empire, valued at two and a half asses (a quarter of a denarius).
ety: From Latin sēstertius (“that is two-and-a-half”), from sēmis (“half”) + tertius (“third”), in which “third” refers to the third as: the sestertius was worth two full asses and half of a third.

senses: An event where amateur radio operators can meet up and trade equipment.
examples: A morning at my local hamfest got me a low-band transceiver (everybody called it a "rice box") for what seemed to me a very reasonable price. The antenna, however, was a more difficult problem.

senses: A kind of landscape design for arid regions, minimising the need for irrigation.
ety: From 1980s Xeriscape, a term coined (and trademarked) by Denver Water. From xeri- + -scape.

senses: A gram-positive bacterium, Streptococcus pneumoniae, that causes pneumonia and other infectious diseases
The study of past ecologies by using the evidence of fossils
A musical instrument consisting of a flat sounding box with numerous strings placed on a horizontal surface, played with a plectrum or fingertips.
Related or similar instruments in other cultures, such as the Chinese guqin or Norwegian harpeleik; especially any chordophone without a neck, and with strings that pass over the body.
ety: Borrowed from German Zither, from Old High German zithara, from Latin cithara, from Ancient Greek κιθάρα (kithára, “a kind of harp”). Doublet of cithara, cither, and guitar.

senses: The process or act of sequestering; a putting aside or separating.
A budget cut resulting from a separation of funding mechanisms.
ety: From Middle French sequestration, from Late Latin sequestrātiō, from Latin sequestrō (“sequester”).
examples: At that time there was no rigid sequestration on the islands, and lepers, if they chose, were allowed to go free.
The company took a revenue hit when sequestration dried up some of its best contracts.

senses: The traditional custom of a Hindu woman giving herself up to be cremated on her husband’s funeral pyre as a sign of her devotion.
ety: From Sanskrit सती (satī́, “good and virtuous or faithful wife”), from सत् (sát, “true, good, right etc.”). In English usage since 1786. Doublet of sin.

senses: The act or process of fetishizing.
examples: To put it epigrammatically, fetishization of the commodity is accompanied by fantasization of the self.

senses: An account of a voyage, particularly those of Hanno and Arrian, recording ports and coastal landmarks.
A voyage along a coast.
Synonym of circuit: the path or distance around a coast.
Synonym of circumnavigation: a voyage around an island or the world.
ety: From Latin periplūs (“account of a voyage”) and Ancient Greek περίπλους (períplous, “voyage, naval manouver, account of a voyage”), from περί (perí, “peri-: around”) + πλοῦς (ploûs, “voyage”), from πλεῖν (pleîn, “to sail”). Cf. French périple, Spanish periplo, & Italian periplo.

senses: Not meritorious; without merit.
examples: Justice Scalia’s comments echoed the often-heard complaints of the defense bar that shareholder litigation poses such a threat to a public company that it forces the defendant to settle even unmeritorious lawsuits.
